title: P0 hosted API ratecap rollout regression investigation
summary: On 2026-03-28 we experienced a P0 degradation of the hosted API manifested as sudden token-level rate caps causing elevated p99/p50 latency, increase in 5xx streaming failures, and request queuing across gateway layer. The incident began after a staged rollout of a new rate-limiter configuration and a throttling service binary change. Impact persisted for ~2h until a rollback and emergency config override restored baseline behavior. This document captures the timeline, root cause analysis, mitigations, and follow-up actions.
impact: Customer-facing API calls to the hosted inference endpoints (text generation and streaming) saw 30-60% increase in tail latency and a spike of 5xx errors (mainly 503/429) across multiple regions. Active requests experienced streaming interruptions and truncated responses. Estimated customer-facing error budget burn: high; several enterprise customers reported degraded UX. Internal churn: on-call SREs and runtime team paged; temporary support escalations.

2026-03-29 14:00 UTC - Drafting of this investigation started.
detection_and_response: Detection was via existing latency SLO alerts and an automated error-rate threshold. Initial on-call diagnostics pointed to increased queue depth at the gateway and elevated per-client throttle counts. The SRE and Serving Runtime on-call teams coordinated: SRE increased front-end capacity, Serving Runtime paged the rollout owner to verify recent deploys. We used temporary config override to bypass new throttle path and then rolled back the rl-service release once correlation was confirmed. Key response actions: 1) open incident channel, 2) increase gateway replica count, 3) record live metrics and logs to incident channel, 4) apply config bypass, 5) rollback release, 6) post-rollback verification and alert tuning.
root_cause: Two contributing changes coincided: (A) rl-service v2.17 introduced a change in token-bucket aggregation logic that unintentionally applied a stricter default max-burst and lowered per-token refill rate when a new header (x-rdwd-client-class) was absent. Canary config implicitly relied on the header being present; an edge in our gateway stripped that header for certain client flows, causing those flows to be classified into the new default (low-cap) bucket. (B) The rollout gating did not include a synthetic workload exercising long-running streaming requests, so the regression in streaming behavior was not caught in canary. The combined effect: legitimate steady streaming traffic was severely throttled, causing request queuing, increased router backpressure, and 5xx failures when client timeouts were hit.
immediate_mitigations:
- Applied temporary config override to force pre-v2.17 rate-limiter behavior for hosted-api routes.
- Rolled back rl-service to v2.16 in affected regions.
- Scaled gateway and proxy layers by +30% during mitigation window.
- Re-enabled header forwarding rule to preserve x-rdwd-client-class for upstream routing.
- Increased retention on per-request traces for deeper post-incident analysis.
long_term_fixes:
- Revert-and-fix: rl-service will release v2.18 that restores previous aggregation semantics and adds explicit handling for missing x-rdwd-client-class header.
- Add end-to-end synthetic canary tests that include streaming workloads and exercise long-tail token consumption patterns.
- Update rollout gating: require streaming-aware performance checks and a gradual rollout with per-tenant throttling verification.
- Improve observability: add a dedicated dashboard showing per-client token-bucket fill/refill rates, burst events, and header propagation stats.
- Add integration test in CI to validate header forwarding behavior across gateway/proxy matrix.
- Implement a safety circuit: if token-bucket-derived rejection rate exceeds threshold for >2min, automatically revert to previous config or open a soft bypass.

lessons_learned:
- Canaries must include workload shapes representative of streaming and long-lived requests, not just short synchronous calls.
- Feature rollouts that add classification logic (headers, client classes) create high risk if the system does not treat missing metadata as a safe fallback.
- Observability gaps: we lacked easy-to-read per-client refill metrics to quickly spot token-bucket misallocation.
- Rollout policy: require a 'kill-switch' and automatic rollback criterion based on per-route rejection/error bursts.
- Documentation/runbooks need concrete queries and a checklist for emergency bypass to avoid ad-hoc commands during high-severity incidents.
appendix:
Key dashboards used: hosted-api-traces, gateway-queue-depth, rl-service-token-buckets, streaming-error-rates.
Relevant PRs and tickets: GH PR #8421 (rl-service change), JIRA SRE-7123 (incident record), GH Issue #8467 (header-forwarding regression).
Example queries: token_bucket_rejects_total{route="/v1/generate"} and token_bucket_fill_rate_bucket{client_class=~".*"}.
On-call notes: during mitigation we observed correlation between clients lacking x-rdwd-client-class header and elevated rejects; a small percentage of traffic (8-12%) was affected but those were predominantly streaming flows which increased their relative error impact.
Customer impact notes: CS tracked three enterprise customers with elevated errors; all received proactive outreach within 90 minutes of mitigation.
